To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human SULT1As do not contribute to DNA adduct formation in vivo after treatment with aristolochic acides and 3-NBA.
the role of the SULT1A family in AA bioactivation is not supported by our data.
human sulfotransferease 1A enzymes do not contribute to the metabolic activation pathways of aristolochate toxins, but are important for bioactivation of 3-nitrobensanthrone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of human and mouse sulfotransferases in the activation of AA and other carcinogenic aromatic nitrosamines in vivo and in vitro.
the elucidation of the role of the human sulfotransfares SULT1A2 and SULT1A3 in the activation pathways for the nephrotoxic and carcinogenic aristolochic compounds AAI and AA-II.
the role of human and mouse SULT1A in the bioactivation of AA and 3-NBA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
human SULT1As play a minor role in the activation of AAI in vivo.
human SULT1 enzymes are not important contributors to AAN/BEN.
SULT1A is not involved in AAI and AA II bioactivation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of SULT1 enzymes on the bioactivity of AA and 3-NBA is tissue-specific and compound-specific.
the contribution of SULT1 enzymes to the activation of AA and 3-NBA in vivo depends on the specific compound.
the role of SULT1 enzymes in DNA adduct formation depends strongly on the chemical structure of the substrate and on the target tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in vivo bioactivation of aromatic compounds is not always reflected by in vitro assays.
the role of SULT1 enzymes in the activation of AA and other compounds may be difficult to predict and needs to be investigated in detail for each compound of interest.
genetic modulation of human SULT enzymes is not sufficient to explain the differences in the genotoxic potency of AAI observed in vitro.
